title: You probably skipped him.
paragraphs: You probably skipped him.

Be honest—you’ve read the story of King David running for his life, betrayed by his own son, humiliated, barefoot, weeping… and your eyes locked onto the drama. The rebellion. The heartbreak. The collapse of a kingdom.
But not him.
He was there, standing in the dust, watching a broken king walk away from everything.
And he had every reason to leave.
His name was Ittai the Gittite.
A foreigner. An outsider. A man who didn’t grow up in Israel, didn’t inherit the promises, didn’t owe David anything. He had just arrived. Just pledged himself. No history. No roots. No obligation.
And yet when David turned to him and said, “Why will you also go with us? Go back… you are a foreigner… return and stay with the king,” something happened that most people miss.
Because that’s what makes sense, right?

Stay where it’s safe.
Align with power.
Protect yourself.
David even gave him an honorable exit. No guilt. No pressure. No expectation.
You could walk away clean.
And that’s exactly where most people would have left.
Because when following starts to cost something, loyalty gets re-evaluated.
But Ittai didn’t move.

He didn’t calculate.
He didn’t negotiate.
He didn’t hesitate.
He answered with words that cut through centuries:
“As the Lord lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life, there also will your servant be.” (2 Samuel 15:21)
Read that again.
Death or life.

Not comfort or blessing.
Not victory or reward.
Death… or life.

That’s not convenience.
That’s not emotional hype.
That’s not temporary excitement.
That’s covenant-level loyalty from a man who had no covenant.
Let that confront you.
Because you say you follow Christ.

But what happens when the path looks like loss instead of gain?
When obedience isolates you?
When standing with Him costs your reputation, your relationships, your comfort?
You start negotiating.
You start redefining “faithfulness.”
You start saying things like, “God understands…”
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Ittai wasn’t just pledging himself to David.
He was revealing something deeper—something that exposes us.

Because thousands in Israel had history with David.
They saw his victories.
They sang his songs.
They benefited from his reign.
And when pressure came…
They left.
But the outsider stayed.
The one who owed nothing… gave everything.
God saw it.
You knew.

That quiet moment where you chose distance over devotion.
Where following Jesus felt optional because it became uncomfortable.

You didn’t say it out loud, but your life said it clearly:
“I’ll follow… as long as it doesn’t cost me too much.”
And that’s where this breaks open.
Because Jesus never hid the cost.
“If anyone would come after Me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me.” (Luke 9:23)

A cross is not symbolic comfort.
It’s death.
So when you say you follow Him, what you’re really saying is:
“I’m willing to stay… even when it feels like I’m losing.”
That’s where most turn back.
But not Ittai.
And not the ones who have truly seen Christ.
Because when you realize who Jesus is—crucified for your sin, risen for your justification, offering grace you didn’t earn—you stop calculating what it costs you…
And you start surrendering because of what it cost Him.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.

David was a shadow.
Jesus is the King.
And unlike David, Jesus didn’t just walk into exile…
He walked into death.
For you.
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)
You weren’t loyal first.
He was.
You didn’t stay.
He did.
So now the question isn’t whether you can walk away.
The question is why you still want to.
Because there are only two paths in front of you:
A life where you follow Jesus when it’s easy… and slowly drift when it’s not.
Or a life where you say—like Ittai—
“Wherever You are… I stay.”
Even if it costs.
Especially if it costs.
That kind of loyalty doesn’t come from effort.
It comes from repentance.

From finally admitting:
“I’ve been following at a distance.”
And turning back.
Say it plainly.
“I haven’t been loyal.”
Type it if you need to. Let it come into the light.
And if you know someone who’s drifting, someone who only follows when it’s convenient… send this to them. Not to judge them—but because you see where it leads.
Stay close to this. You’ll need this reminder again when following starts to feel costly.
And if you’re done playing surface-level Christianity… there’s a deeper walk waiting.
Because in the end, the overlooked ones…
Are often the ones who were truly faithful.
